questions.text: An architect learns that a building material supplier is willing to offer a 4% price discount on products specified in the architect's design. The supplier requests that the architect NOT disclose this discount to the client. The architect should:

options.text: Accept the arrangement because the client will still receive a quality product, assuming the discount does not affect the overall project budget negatively
Negotiate a higher discount percentage and then disclose it to the client, ensuring transparency and adherence to ethical standards
Refuse the arrangement; any discount must be credited to the client per Section 5.2, not concealed
Accept the arrangement only if the product quality is demonstrably superior to alternatives, and the discount does not compromise the project's integrity

rationale.a: Product quality is irrelevant to the violation. Section 5.2 requires discounts to be credited to the client; concealment for third-party benefit violates professional ethics regardless of quality.
rationale.b: Negotiating a higher discount does not cure the violation if it is not credited to the client. Section 5.2 is explicit about the beneficiary of market advantages.
rationale.d: Superior quality does not justify nondisclosure. Section 5.2 mandates that all market benefits be transferred to the client; product excellence cannot override this requirement.
rationale.correct: Article IV, Section 5.2 states: 'Any market discount shall be credited to the Client.' Concealing a discount to benefit the supplier or architect violates Section 4.6 (compensation only through fees) and Section 4.9 (disclosure of business conditions affecting the client).
rationale.takeaway: Market discounts are permissible ONLY if credited to the client. Concealment converts a legitimate discount into prohibited remuneration.

questions.text: An architect is offered 6% of project costs by a preferred contractor in exchange for recommending the contractor to clients. If the architect accepts this offer, the primary violation is:

options.text: The percentage is too high (should be 3% or less) according to industry standards for referral fees in similar contexts
The architect did not consult with the contractor association before accepting, which is a recommended practice to ensure transparency and avoid conflicts of interest
Section 4.6 is violated: the architect accepted compensation from an 'interested source' other than the client
The arrangement violates tax regulations, not professional ethics, as it may lead to undeclared income and potential tax evasion issues

rationale.a: The percentage amount is irrelevant to the ethical violation. Section 4.6 prohibits commissions from interested sources entirely, not just those above a certain threshold.
rationale.b: Consulting an association would not cure the violation. Section 4.6 creates an absolute prohibition on accepting compensation from interested sources.
rationale.d: This conflates tax compliance with professional ethics. While tax treatment matters, the primary violation is ethical under Section 4.6—the architect's compensation sources are regulated by professional conduct.
rationale.correct: Section 4.6 prohibits accepting 'any other returns in whatever form from any interested source other than the Client.' A contractor is an interested source. Any percentage commission, regardless of size, violates this prohibition.
rationale.takeaway: The issue is not the percentage—it's that third-party compensation is inherently conflicted and prohibited by the Code.

questions.text: Section 4.6 of the Code states that an architect's compensation shall be:

options.text: Derived from multiple sources including client fees and supplier commissions, allowing for flexibility in income generation
Solely through professional fee charged directly to the client, with no other returns from any interested source
Supplemented by market commissions from contractors and material suppliers, which can lead to conflicts of interest
Negotiated individually for each project to maximize architect income, providing opportunities for tailored compensation packages

rationale.a: This violates Section 4.6's explicit prohibition on multiple compensation sources. The architect cannot accept returns from any interested source other than the Client, making dual-source compensation prohibited.
rationale.c: Market commissions from suppliers are prohibited by Section 4.6. The only permitted supplier benefit is a market discount that must be credited to the client (Section 5.2); direct commissions to the architect are prohibited.
rationale.d: While fees are negotiated per project, Section 4.6 does not allow maximization through outside sources. The method is restricted to professional fees charged directly to the Client.
rationale.correct: Section 4.6 explicitly states: 'The Architect shall be compensated for his services solely through his professional fee charged directly to the Client. He shall not accept nor ask for any other returns in whatever form from any interested source other than the Client.' This is a core rule to prevent conflicts of interest.
rationale.takeaway: Sole-source compensation rule: client only. No exceptions except market discounts credited to client per Section 5.2.

questions.text: An architect designs a commercial building and later agrees with the developer to serve as the general contractor and construct the building for a fixed lump sum of 800 million pesos. According to Section 4.8, this arrangement is:

options.text: Permissible because the architect is qualified to manage construction and has the necessary experience
Permissible only if the architect discloses the dual role to all stakeholders and obtains their consent
Prohibited because Section 4.8 forbids fixed-sum construction contracts for projects where the architect serves as Architect-of-Record
Permissible if the architect obtains a separate contractor's license and complies with all regulatory requirements

rationale.a: Qualifications are irrelevant to the categorical prohibition. The conflict is not about competence but about the inherent tension between fixed-sum construction and the designer's role as the client's quality advocate.
rationale.b: Disclosure does not cure this specific violation. Section 4.8 absolutely prohibits this combination; disclosure cannot convert a prohibited arrangement into a permitted one.
rationale.d: A contractor's license does not cure the fundamental conflict prohibited by Section 4.8. The combination of roles for a single project is the issue, regardless of external licensing.
rationale.correct: Section 4.8 states: 'The Architect shall not undertake, under a fixed contract sum agreement, the construction of any project based on plans and specifications prepared by him in his capacity as the Architect-of-Record.' This avoids the conflict between the designer's quality oversight and the contractor's profit motive under a fixed sum.
rationale.takeaway: Architect-of-Record + architect-contractor under fixed-sum = prohibited conflict of interest. Design and construction cannot be combined this way for the same project.

questions.text: A developer offers to make an architect a passive investor in a residential project (no involvement in design or management). The architect would receive profit-sharing but no fee for architectural services. The architect should:

options.text: Accept because passive investment does not affect professional judgment, assuming no conflict of interest arises from the investment
Accept if the development company is not a client on this specific project, ensuring that there is no overlap with existing professional obligations
Decline or fully disclose the investment to the client because Section 4.9 requires disclosure of 'any business interest which will relate to, or affect the interest of his Client'
Accept as long as the profit-sharing percentage is reasonable, provided that it does not compromise the architect's ethical responsibilities

rationale.a: Passive status does not eliminate conflict under Section 4.9. A profit-sharing interest in the developer creates potential bias, affecting the architect's standing as an impartial adviser regardless of claimed passivity.
rationale.b: Lack of an active client relationship on that specific project does not cure the conflict. Section 4.9 requires disclosure of business interests that 'will relate to' the client's interest; interest in a developer affects judgment toward that entity.
rationale.d: The amount of profit-sharing is irrelevant to the disclosure obligation. Section 4.9 prohibits undisclosed business interests that could weaken professional standing as an impartial adviser.
rationale.correct: Section 4.9 requires disclosure of 'any business interest which will relate to, or affect the interest of his Client' and any interest that might weaken his standing as an unprejudiced adviser. A profit-sharing interest in a development project creates potential conflicts regarding design decisions, costs, and specifications.
rationale.takeaway: Financial interest in projects or development companies must be disclosed, even if 'passive.' Potential for bias is the standard, not actual bias.

questions.text: Section 4.3 obligates the architect to advise a client against proceeding with a project if the project is impractical due to financial, legal, or other exigent conditions. The architect's obligation to provide this advice exists even if:

options.text: The client expressly insists on proceeding despite the architect's concerns
The advice means the loss of a prospective commission to the architect
The architect has already been paid the full design fee
The project will cause minor inconvenience to the architect's other work

rationale.a: The architect's duty to advise is unconditional. Even if the client insists on proceeding, the architect must provide the professional warning. Section 4.3 does not allow the architect to withhold advice based on client resistance.
rationale.c: Payment of fees does not terminate the duty to advise. If the project becomes impractical during design, Section 4.3 requires continued advice; the architect cannot remain silent because they were already paid.
rationale.d: Project convenience is irrelevant. The architect's personal schedule cannot override the duty to advise the client against an impractical project.
rationale.correct: Section 4.3 explicitly states: 'The Architect shall advise a Client against proceeding with any project whose practicability may be questionable... even if such advice may mean the loss of a prospective commission to the Architect.' Professional integrity must supersede fee maximization.
rationale.takeaway: Loyalty to client = duty to give unwelcome but truthful advice, regardless of financial impact on the architect.

questions.text: According to the Code of Ethical Conduct, the architect-client relationship is founded on:

options.text: Contractual obligation and payment terms
Trust, confidence, and mutual moral obligations
The architect's professional standing and experience
The client's ability to pay the full professional fee

rationale.a: While contracts govern services, Article II Section 3 explicitly establishes that the relationship is founded on trust and confidence, not just contractual terms. The Code creates moral obligations that exist beyond and above contract provisions.
rationale.c: The architect's standing supports capacity to serve but does not establish the relationship's foundation. The Code makes clear the foundation is trust and moral obligations, not credentials alone.
rationale.d: The client's financial capacity is a practical consideration but not the foundation of the relationship. The Code grounds the relationship in moral obligations independent of payment ability.
rationale.correct: Article II, Section 3 of the Code (SPP Document 200) states: 'The Architect’s relation to his Client is based on trust and confidence. To insure the continued existence of such state of good relationship, the Architect’s position carries with it certain moral obligations to his Client and to himself.' This establishes trust and moral obligation as the foundation.
rationale.takeaway: The relationship is fiduciary, not purely contractual. Moral obligations run deeper than contract terms.

questions.text: Section 4.9 of the Code requires that an architect with a personal financial interest in a building materials company:

options.text: Must stop practicing architecture until the interest is sold
Shall inform the client of the business interest that could affect the client's interests
May continue practice without disclosure if the interest does not directly profit from the specific project
Can use the materials provided the price is competitive with other suppliers

rationale.a: The Code does not mandate cessation of practice. The requirement is disclosure, which allows the architect to continue if the client consents after full information.
rationale.c: Non-profit on a specific project does not cure the conflict under Section 4.9. The test is whether the interest 'will relate to, or affect' the client's interest; potential for conflict exists regardless of realized profit.
rationale.d: Competitive pricing does not satisfy the disclosure requirement. Even at competitive prices, a financial interest in the supplier presents a potential conflict that must be disclosed.
rationale.correct: Section 4.9 states: 'If the Architect has any business interest which will relate to, or affect the interest of his Client, he should inform his Client of such condition or situation.' The test is whether the interest could affect client interests or weaken the architect's standing as an unprejudiced adviser.
rationale.takeaway: Disclosure is the remedy. The architect can continue practicing but MUST inform the client of potential conflicts.

questions.text: An architect receives a fee of 15 million pesos for planning services. Seeking to retain further work, they offer to reduce this planning fee by 5 million pesos if allowed to also design the residential buildings on the site. According to Section 4.2 and Section 7.2, this offer is:

options.text: Acceptable because it provides the developer with cost savings, which can be beneficial for project budget management
Unethical because it constitutes fee undercutting that violates Section 7.2's prohibition on competing on professional charges
Acceptable if the architect's reduced fee is still based on the Basic Minimum Fee standard, ensuring compliance with professional guidelines
Permissible as part of negotiation for a larger scope of services, provided all parties agree to the revised terms

rationale.a: Cost savings do not justify unethical competition. Section 7.2 prohibits competing 'on the basis of difference of professional charges' regardless of whether the client benefits financially.
rationale.c: Even if the resulting fee meets minimum standards, the act of using a fee reduction to win work from a competitor is the violation of Section 7.2.
rationale.d: This mischaracterizes the transaction. While scope expansion might justify adjustment, the motive here is price undercutting to defeat a competitor, which is prohibited.
rationale.correct: Section 7.2 states: 'The Architect shall not knowingly compete with other Architects on the basis of difference of professional charges.' By offering a reduction to win a commission being considered for others, the architect is engaging in prohibited fee competition. Section 4.2 requires fees to be commensurate with professional standing and the Basic Minimum Fee.
rationale.takeaway: Fee competition violates Section 7.2. Architects cannot reduce fees to win work away from others. Fees must reflect work value, not competitive undercutting.

questions.text: An architect discovers that the client's budget is insufficient for the project scope. The client states: 'Just proceed with the design; I'll decide later what to reduce.' The architect's best course of action per Section 4.3 is:

options.text: Proceed with design as requested; the client has assumed the risk and any subsequent scope reduction is the client's sole responsibility
Advise the client in writing of the impracticability, document the advice, and proceed only with written acknowledgment from the client
Refuse to proceed until the client obtains additional funding or secures a revised financing plan approved by the lending institution
Proceed but reduce scope unilaterally to match the budget without client consultation, relying on the architect's professional judgment alone

rationale.a: Proceeding without written documentation of the architect's advice violates the spirit of Section 4.3. Merely accepting a verbal assurance does not satisfy the requirement to provide professional advice on practicality.
rationale.c: Section 4.3 does not strictly mandate refusal to proceed; it mandates providing advice against proceeding. The client may choose to continue, but the architect must ensure the advice is delivered and documented.
rationale.d: Unilateral scope reduction violates the duty of consultation. Section 4.3 requires the architect to inform the client of the situation; the client must make the final decision on scope adjustment.
rationale.correct: Section 4.3 requires: 'The Architect shall advise a Client against proceeding with any project whose practicability may be questionable due to financial or legal important and/or exigent conditions...' The architect must fulfill this duty to advise by providing it in writing and documenting the risk to the client.
rationale.takeaway: Duty to advise = duty to document. Proceeding requires ensuring the client has received the professional advice regarding project viability.
